Nx handles task orchestration (build, test, lint) with caching and dependency-aware execution order. 62→ 63→Module boundary rules: `client` has no dependency on `parser` or `diff`. `parser` imports only from `client/types`. `diff` imports only from `parser/types`. The barrel `src/index.ts` is the sole public surface — no internal module paths are exported. Nx enforce-module-boundaries lint rule should be configured to enforce these constraints. 64→ 65→--- 66→ 67→## 2. HTML Parsing Library 68→ 69→**Options evaluated:** 70→ 71→| Library | Mechanism | Key property | 72→|---|---|---| 73→| `htmlparser2` | SAX-style streaming + DomHandler tree builder | Exposes `startIndex`/`endIndex` on every token | 74→| `cheerio` | Wraps parse5 (or htmlparser2) with jQuery API | No native byte-offset access on nodes | 75→| `linkedom` | WHATWG DOM in Node.js | No position data on nodes | 76→| `parse5` | Full WHATWG-spec tree builder | No position data by default | 77→| `node-html-parser` | Lightweight, exposes `range` on nodes | Less actively maintained | 78→ 79→**Recommendation: `htmlparser2`.** 80→ 81→The core requirement is character-level source mappings on every node (section 3). `htmlparser2` uniquely exposes `startIndex` and `endIndex` on each token during SAX parsing — available at parse time with no second pass, no heuristic substring search. We build a minimal DOM-like tree during the SAX pass (via `DomHandler`) with position data attached directly to each node. 82→ 83→Cheerio, linkedom, and parse5 are convenient for querying but require post-hoc position reconstruction by searching the original HTML string for node content — fragile when SEC filing HTML contains repeated boilerplate paragraphs. `htmlparser2`'s position data is authoritative; derived reconstruction is not. 84→ 85→--- 86→ 87→## 3. Source Mapping Strategy 88→ 89→### Options Evaluated 90→ 91→**A. Byte offsets** — Each node stores `{ start: number, end: number }` as character offsets into the original HTML string. Directly available from `htmlparser2`. Serializes as JSON integers. Enables `html.slice(start, end)`. The web app can inject highlight spans by preprocessing the HTML string before rendering. 92→ 93→**B. DOM path references** — XPath or CSS nth-child paths (e.g., `body > div:nth-child(3) > p:nth-child(2)`). Browser-native; drives `document.querySelector`. Fragile when DOM structure differs between old/new filing versions. Requires browser re-parse and query — adds coupling to Epic 2's rendering model. 94→ 95→**C. Both** — Byte offsets as canonical, DOM paths derived on demand. 96→ 97→### Recommendation: Byte offsets as the canonical source map. 98→ 99→Rationale: 100→1. `htmlparser2` provides them at zero cost during parsing. 101→2. The diff engine operates server-side on strings — offsets are the natural representation. 102→3. The web app (Epic 2) can inject highlights by slicing and reassembling the HTML string before `innerHTML` assignment, which is simpler than DOM path queries on a re-parsed document. 103→4. DOM paths can be derived from offsets later; the reverse is not true. 104→ 105→Note: `htmlparser2` indices are character positions (JS UTF-16 string indices), not raw byte offsets. Spike A must document this distinction for any `Buffer`-based consumers. 106→ 107→```typescript 108→export interface SourceLocation { 109→ /** Character offset of the opening `<` in the original HTML string (JS string index). */ 110→ start: number; 111→ /** Character offset one past the last character of this node's closing tag. */ 112→ end: number; 113→} 114→ 115→export interface SourceMapped { 116→ source: SourceLocation; 117→ /** Raw HTML substring. Only populated when parseOptions.includeSourceHtml is true. */ 118→ sourceHtml?: string; 119→} 120→``` 121→ 122→--- 123→ 124→## 4. Diff Algorithm 125→ 126→### Options Evaluated 127→ 128→**A. Myers diff** — Standard O(ND) algorithm. Minimizes edit distance. No content awareness — treats each paragraph as an opaque token. Produces noisy output when sections move or when large unchanged blocks appear between two changed paragraphs. 129→ 130→**B. Patience diff** — Preprocessing layer over Myers. Identifies tokens appearing exactly once in both versions as anchors, divides documents at anchors, applies Myers recursively on each segment. Common unique paragraphs (specific legal boilerplate, financial labels) become natural anchors in SEC filings. 131→ 132→**C. Custom section aligner + patience diff** — Two phases: (1) match sections using normalized heading similarity; (2) within matched section pairs, run patience diff on paragraphs. Does not treat the document as a flat token stream. 133→ 134→### Recommendation: Custom section aligner (phase 1) + patience diff (phase 2). 135→ 136→The section-level alignment problem is not a standard line-diff problem. 10-K filings have standardized headings ("Item 1A. Risk Factors") that are stable across years. Running any line diff across a full document would align by proximity, not semantic identity — sections that moved position would appear as mass-delete followed by mass-insert. 137→ 138→The custom aligner uses Jaro-Winkler similarity on normalized heading text (lowercased, "item 1a" normalization). Threshold ~0.75: above = same section (possibly modified), below = added or removed. This handles renames ("Risk Factors" → "Risk Factors and Uncertainties") as modifications rather than delete+add pairs. 139→ 140→Within matched sections, patience diff (via the `diff` npm package) operates on paragraph text. Patience is preferred over raw Myers because SEC filings reuse boilerplate — unique paragraphs become anchors that keep the diff aligned even when new paragraphs are inserted nearby. For sentence-level diffs within modified paragraphs, Myers on sentence tokens is acceptable (sentences are short enough that Myers is not noisy at that granularity). 141→ 142→Spike B validates the similarity threshold and output quality before committing this approach. 143→ 144→--- 145→ 146→## 5. value: string }>; 231→ sourceMapping: DiffRange; 232→} 233→ 234→export interface TableDiff { 235→ changeType: ChangeType; 236→ oldTable?: Table; 237→ newTable?: Table; 238→ cellDiffs?: Array<{ 239→ row: number; col: number; 240→ changeType: Exclude; 241→ oldValue?: string; newValue?: string; 242→ sourceMapping: DiffRange; 243→ }>; 244→ sourceMapping: DiffRange; 245→} 246→ 247→export interface SectionDiff { 248→ id: string; heading: string; changeType: ChangeType; 249→ oldSection?: FilingSection; newSection?: FilingSection; 250→ paragraphDiffs: ParagraphDiff[]; 251→ tableDiffs: TableDiff[]; 252→ subsectionDiffs: SectionDiff[]; 253→ sourceMapping: DiffRange; 254→} 255→ 256→export interface StructuredDiff { 257→ oldFiling: RawFiling; 258→ newFiling: RawFiling; 259→ sectionDiffs: SectionDiff[]; 260→ summary: { added: number; removed: number; modified: number; unchanged: number; reordered: number }; 261→ generatedAt: Temporal.Instant; 262→} 263→ 264→// ---- Function signatures ---- 265→ 266→export declare function createEdgarClient(options: EdgarClientOptions): { 267→ fetchFiling(accessionNumber: string): Promise; 268→}; 269→export declare function parseFiling( 270→ raw: RawFiling, 271→ options?: { includeSourceHtml?: boolean; logger?: Logger }, 272→): StructuredDocument; 273→export declare function diffFilings( 274→ oldDoc: StructuredDocument, 275→ newDoc: StructuredDocument, 276→): StructuredDiff; 277→ 278→export interface Logger { warn(msg: string): void; } 279→``` 280→ 281→--- 282→ 283→## 6. HTML Pattern Catalog 284→ 285→SEC filings are produced by various filing agents (DFIN, Toppan Merrill, Workiva, and others) whose HTML templates are undocumented. Rather than attempting to detect and branch on the filing agent, the parser uses a single heuristic-based approach that handles all observed heading patterns generically. 286→ 287→**Cataloging steps:** 288→ 289→1. Collect 10-15 sample 10-K filings from a variety of large-cap filers. Aim for diversity in HTML structure rather than targeting specific agents. 290→2. For each filing, document the HTML patterns used for section headings — element types (`

`–`

`, `

`, `

`), inline styles (bold, uppercase, font-size), CSS classes, and structural conventions (table-of-contents presence, page breaks). 291→3. Commit findings to `.specs/epic-1-library/html-patterns.md` as a structured catalog of observed heading patterns. 292→4. Build a single `section-extractor.ts` that applies a ranked set of heuristics: (a) scan for elements matching `ITEM \d+[A-Z]?` in normalized text, (b) weight matches by heading signals (h-tag > bold > uppercase > plain), (c) use scoring to break ties when multiple candidates match. 293→ 294→**Risk gate (per PRD):** If more than 3 distinct HTML pattern families are needed and the heuristic approach can't cover them reliably (< 80% section detection accuracy across sample filings), escalate the parser to its own epic. 295→ 296→--- 297→ 298→## 7. Error Handling Strategy 299→ 300→**Network (client layer):** `EdgarNetworkError` with `statusCode` and `retryAfter`. Client retries 429/503 with exponential backoff (3 attempts, 1s base). Callers see the error only after all retries fail. The internal token bucket enforces 10 req/s — callers do not see rate-limit errors under normal operation. 301→ 302→**Parse (parser layer):** Parser never throws on valid HTML. Unrecognized sections go into `id: 'unrecognized'` catch-all. Structural anomalies are collected in `StructuredDocument.parseWarnings`. A pluggable `Logger` (default: no-op) accepts warnings via `parseFiling(raw, { logger })`. 303→ 304→**Diff (diff layer):** No recoverable failure paths. Unmatched sections are emitted as added/removed pairs with no content diffs. 305→ 306→```typescript 307→export class EdgarNetworkError extends Error { 308→ readonly name = 'EdgarNetworkError'; 309→ constructor( 310→ public readonly statusCode: number, 311→ public readonly accessionNumber: string, 312→ public readonly retryAfter?: number, 313→ ) { super(`EDGAR returned ${statusCode} for ${accessionNumber}`); } 314→} 315→``` 316→ 317→--- 318→ 319→## 8. Testing Approach 320→ 321→### Unit Tests (`tests/unit/`) 322→ 323→Test individual pure functions. HTML fixtures are inline tagged-template strings inside each test file — no external files for unit tests. Keep each fixture under 30 lines of HTML. Cover: section heading detection across HTML pattern variations (h-tags, bold, uppercase, font tags), table cell colspan/rowspan normalization, Jaro-Winkler threshold calibration, source offset arithmetic edge cases (empty elements, self-closing tags, comments). 324→ 325→### Integration Tests (`tests/integration/`) 326→ 327→Real SEC HTML files committed to `tests/integration/fixtures/`. Naming: `{formtype}-{ticker}-{year}.html` (e.g., `10k-aapl-2023.html`). Start with 6-8 files covering diverse HTML structures. Assertions: (a) correct section count for a known filing, (b) specific section IDs present (`item-1a`, `item-7`), (c) source offset round-trip: `html.slice(section.source.start, section.source.end)` contains the section heading text. Diff integration tests: parse two consecutive annual filings for the same company, run `diffFilings`, assert summary counts are non-zero and no exception is thrown. 328→ 329→### Fuzz / Structural Variation Tests (`tests/fuzz/`) 330→ 331→A `FilingHtmlGenerator` generates structurally plausible but randomized 10-K HTML: random Item ordering, mixed heading styles (h2/bold-p/uppercase-p), tables with random colspan/rowspan values (including pathological overlap), empty sections, sections with duplicate headings, Unicode in heading text. Generate N=200 synthetic filings per CI run. For each, assert invariants: (a) no uncaught exception, (b) `sections.length >= 0` (empty is allowed), (c) all `source.start < source.end`, (d) all offsets within `[0, html.length)`. This surfaces off-by-one errors, greedy regex matches, and null-dereferences that targeted unit tests miss. 332→ 333→--- 334→ 335→## 9. Spike Tasks 336→ 337→### Spike A: Source Mapping Prototype 338→ 339→**Goal:** Validate that `htmlparser2` `startIndex`/`endIndex` values provide accurate, reliable character-level positions on real SEC HTML before committing this architecture. 340→ 341→**Scope:** Fetch one real 10-K filing from EDGAR. Build a minimal SAX-based parser using `htmlparser2`'s `DomHandler`. Attach `startIndex`/`endIndex` to each node. Identify 5 section boundaries. Verify `html.slice(node.startIndex, node.endIndex)` captures expected content. Test with a filing containing multi-byte characters to clarify character-vs-byte indexing. 342→ 343→**Deliverable:** `spikes/source-mapping/` with runnable TypeScript and `NOTES.md` documenting: (a) character-vs-byte behavior, (b) any CDATA or comment anomalies in SEC HTML, (c) parse time for a full 10-K, (d) API stability across `htmlparser2` versions. 344→ 345→**Success criteria:** All 5 offset checks pass. Multi-byte behavior documented and handled. Parse time < 500ms. 346→ 347→**Fallback:** If `htmlparser2` offsets are unreliable, pivot to two-pass: parse with `linkedom` for structure, reconstruct positions by scanning the original HTML string for each node's outer HTML (with deduplication handling). 348→ 349→**Time box:** 2 days. 350→ 351→### Spike B: Diff Algorithm Prototype 352→ 353→**Goal:** Validate section alignment quality and patience-diff output on real filing pairs before committing the algorithm. 354→ 355→**Scope:** Two consecutive 10-K filing pairs (minimum; use two different companies). Implement custom section aligner with Jaro-Winkler similarity. For matched sections, apply patience diff at the paragraph level via the `diff` npm package. Compare output against naive Myers on the full document text. Manually review alignment and diff output readability. 356→ 357→**Deliverable:** `spikes/diff-algorithm/` with runnable TypeScript and `NOTES.md` documenting: (a) section alignment accuracy per filing pair (correctly matched / total), (b) optimal Jaro-Winkler threshold, (c) paragraph diff quality (subjective: does it highlight meaningful changes?), (d) full-pair performance, (e) cases where patience performs worse than Myers. 358→ 359→**Success criteria:** > 90% section alignment accuracy for both pairs. Paragraph diffs highlight meaningful changes, not whitespace/boilerplate noise. Full diff < 2 seconds per pair. 360→ 361→**Fallback:** If Jaro-Winkler heading similarity is insufficient, add TF-IDF scoring on section content as a secondary alignment signal. 362→ 363→**Time box:** 2 days. 364→ 365→

# Epic 1: SEC Filing Diff Library

## Overview

A library that fetches SEC filings from EDGAR, parses them into a structured document model, and computes structured diffs between two filings. This is the core engine that all downstream consumers (web app, chat, programmatic users) depend on.

## Goals

- Fetch any full-text SEC filing by its accession number from EDGAR
- Parse filings into a normalized, structured document representation with source mappings back to the original HTML
- Produce a structured, section-aware diff between two parsed filings
- Expose a clean programmatic API suitable for embedding in other systems

## Non-Goals

- Web UI or any visual presentation (Epic 2)
- LLM-powered chat or Q&A (Epic 3)
- Real-time filing monitoring or alerting
- Filing search or discovery (listing available filings for a company is a separate concern)
- XBRL parsing or extraction (future epic)
- Local caching of fetched filings (future feature)
- Package distribution (consumed as a local dependency only)

## Target Users

- Developers building on top of the library (including ourselves for Epics 2 and 3)
- Power users who want programmatic access to filing diffs

---

## EDGAR Concepts

The library operates on SEC EDGAR data. Key concepts:

- **CIK (Central Index Key):** A 10-digit numeric identifier assigned by the SEC to every filing entity. Example: `0000320193` (Apple Inc.).
- **Accession Number:** The unique identifier for a specific filing submission. Format: `{filer-CIK}-{YY}-{sequence}`, e.g., `0000320193-23-000106`. The first 10 digits are the CIK of the submitting entity, followed by a 2-digit year and a sequence number.
- **Primary Document:** Each filing submission contains one or more documents. The primary document is the main filing (e.g., the 10-K HTML). It is identified by filename within the submission.
- **Filing URL pattern:** `https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/{CIK}/{accession-number-no-dashes}/{primary-document-filename}`

The SEC provides a free REST API at `data.sec.gov` that returns JSON without authentication. The submissions endpoint (`https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK{padded-cik}.json`) returns a company's filing history including accession numbers, filing dates, form types, and primary document filenames. This API is how callers of our library would discover filing identifiers before passing them to us, but that discovery is outside the scope of this library.

**Rate limit policy:** SEC limits programmatic access to 10 requests/second and requires a `User-Agent` header identifying the caller (format: `"Company Name email@domain.com"`).

---

## User Stories

### EDGAR Client

**US-1.1: Fetch a filing by accession number**
As a developer, I want to fetch a specific SEC filing by providing its accession number so that I can retrieve the full-text document for processing.

Acceptance criteria:
- Accepts an accession number (e.g., `0000320193-23-000106`) as the filing identifier
- Retrieves the primary HTML document from EDGAR Archives
- Returns the raw HTML content along with filing metadata (CIK, form type, filing date, accession number)
- Includes a proper `User-Agent` header as required by SEC

**US-1.2: Respect SEC rate limits**
As a developer, I want the client to respect SEC EDGAR rate limits so that requests don't get blocked.

Acceptance criteria:
- Enforces maximum 10 requests/second to EDGAR endpoints
- Backs off on 429 or 503 responses
- Rate limiting is implemented within the library's HTTP layer (callers should not need to manage this externally)

Note: Rate limiting is a cross-cutting concern. The idiomatic approach for a library is to provide a configurable HTTP client with sensible defaults (built-in rate limiter) while allowing callers to inject their own client if they need different behavior (e.g., a shared rate limiter across multiple library instances).

### Filing Parser

**US-1.3: Parse a filing into structured sections with source mappings**
As a developer, I want to parse a raw HTML filing into a structured document model with pointers back to the original HTML so that I can work with logical sections and later render highlights on the original document.

Acceptance criteria:
- Identifies standard 10-K sections (Item 1, 1A, 1B, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7A, 8, 9, 9A, 9B, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15)
- Handles common HTML patterns for section headings (h-tags, bold paragraphs, font tags, uppercase text)
- Produces a document tree: Document > Section > Subsection > Content blocks (paragraphs, tables, lists)
- Each node in the tree includes source location references (byte offsets or DOM node identifiers) pointing back to the corresponding range in the original HTML
- Source mappings enable downstream consumers to overlay diff highlights on the original HTML rendering
- Handles filings from major filing agents (Donnelley Financial Solutions, Toppan Merrill, Workiva)

Note on filing agents: These three agents cover the vast majority of large-cap SEC filings. They do not publish public documentation on their HTML templates. The practical approach is to collect sample filings from each agent and reverse-engineer the HTML patterns (CSS classes, heading styles, document structure conventions) used for section boundaries.

**US-1.4: Parse tables into structured representations**
As a developer, I want tables in filings to be parsed into a structured row/column model so that table diffs can be computed at the cell level.

Acceptance criteria:
- Extracts HTML tables into a row/column data structure
- Preserves header rows and column labels
- Handles merged cells (colspan/rowspan) gracefully
- Retains numeric values as numbers where detectable
- Each cell includes a source mapping back to its position in the original HTML

### Diff Engine

**US-1.5: Compute a section-level diff between two parsed filings**
As a developer, I want to compute a diff that aligns sections across two filings so that I can see which sections were added, removed, or changed.

Acceptance criteria:
- Matches sections across filings by heading text similarity
- Identifies added sections (present in new filing only)
- Identifies removed sections (present in old filing only)
- Identifies modified sections (present in both, content differs)
- Identifies unchanged sections
- Handles renamed sections (e.g., "Risk Factors" -> "Risk Factors and Uncertainties")
- Handles reordered sections (sections that moved position but are otherwise unchanged or modified)
- Handles subsection-level matching within matched sections

**US-1.6: Compute paragraph-level diffs within matched sections**
As a developer, I want paragraph-level diffs within each section so that I can see exactly which paragraphs changed.

Acceptance criteria:
- Within matched sections, aligns paragraphs and detects additions, deletions, and modifications
- For modified paragraphs, computes sentence-level diffs to show what changed within the paragraph
- Handles paragraph reordering without marking everything as changed
- Diff output includes source mappings so that changes can be rendered as overlays/highlights on the original HTML

**US-1.7: Compute table-level diffs**
As a developer, I want table diffs computed at the cell level so that changes to financial statements and other tables are precise.

Acceptance criteria:
- Matches tables across filings by position and header similarity
- Computes cell-by-cell diffs for matched tables
- Identifies added/removed rows and columns
- Highlights changed cell values

**US-1.8: Produce a structured diff output**
As a developer, I want the complete diff to be a structured data object so that any consumer (UI, summary generator, export tool) can work with it programmatically.

This story integrates the outputs of US-1.5 through US-1.7 into a single coherent diff structure.

Acceptance criteria:
- Diff is returned as a structured object, not rendered text
- Includes metadata: accession numbers, filing dates, form type, CIK
- Each section diff includes the section heading, change type (added/removed/modified/unchanged/reordered), and content diffs
- Paragraph diffs within sections include source mappings to both the old and new filing HTML
- Table diffs are included within their containing sections
- Serializable to JSON for storage or transmission
- Output format is designed to support rendering diff highlights as overlays on the original HTML documents

---

## Technical Considerations

### Parser Architecture: Source Mapping

The parser must maintain a bidirectional relationship between the structured document model and the original HTML. This is critical because:

1. **Rendering:** The web app (Epic 2) will render the original HTML and overlay diff highlights. It will not render the cleaned-up/canonical document model.
2. **Accuracy:** Source mappings let us verify that our structural parsing correctly captured the intended content boundaries.

Each node in the structured document tree should carry:
- `source_start`: byte offset (or DOM path) into the original HTML where this node's content begins
- `source_end`: byte offset (or DOM path) where this node's content ends
- `source_html`: optionally, the raw HTML slice for this node (for debugging and verification)

### Filing Agent HTML Patterns

Major filing agents do not publish public template documentation. The approach is empirical:
- Collect 5-10 sample filings from each of Donnelley Financial Solutions (DFIN), Toppan Merrill, and Workiva
- Catalog the HTML patterns each uses for section headings, subsections, tables, and document structure
- Build a pattern-matching layer that detects which agent produced a filing and applies the appropriate parsing rules
- Track pattern families; if more than 3 distinct families emerge, consider splitting parser work into its own epic

### Parser Risk Signals

If any of these occur, consider splitting the parser into its own epic:
- More than 3 distinct HTML pattern families needed for section detection
- Table parsing requires filing-agent-specific logic for more than 2 agents
- Test coverage across 10 sample filings drops below 80% section detection accuracy

### API Surface

The public API should be minimal. Callers provide specific filing identifiers (accession numbers), not search queries:

```
fetch_filing(accession_number) -> RawFiling
parse_filing(raw_filing) -> StructuredDocument
diff_filings(doc_a, doc_b) -> StructuredDiff
```

Filing discovery (listing/searching filings by company, type, date range) is out of scope for this library. The SEC's submissions API at `data.sec.gov/submissions/` provides this capability and callers can use it directly.

### Technology Decisions (TBD)

- Programming language and package manager
- HTML parsing library
- Diff algorithm (Myers, patience, or custom for section alignment)
- Source mapping strategy (byte offsets vs. DOM node references vs. both)

---

## Open Questions

1. **Language choice** -- What language/runtime should the library target? Python is natural for data work and has strong HTML parsing libraries. TypeScript/Node would align if the web app is JS-based. Rust or Go if performance is a priority.

## Common Issues

**Import Resolution Errors**
One of the most common issues is TypeScript not being able to find imports, which typically appears as "Cannot find module '@my-org/my-lib' or its corresponding type declarations." This often stems from incorrect paths in tsconfig.base.json, where the path aliases may not point to the correct src/index.ts of your library.

**TypeScript Configuration Complexity**
Many developers struggle with managing multiple tsconfig files, as Nx monorepos can have 50+ configuration files scattered throughout the workspace for managing TypeScript across dozens of apps and libraries. Every project's tsconfig.json needs to stay updated with correct references to its dependencies, requiring manual management of the TypeScript project graph.

**Module Configuration Errors**
A common error developers encounter is related to the compilerOptions.module property being set to invalid values like "preserve".

**Path Aliases vs Project References**
Large monorepos using TypeScript path aliases can struggle with slowness, memory issues, and editors not being able to properly resolve symbols. For larger Nx monorepos, TypeScript Project References are recommended because Nx heavily relies on them for its build system and caching, making them the expert choice for performance and type safety.

**Custom Build Pipeline Challenges**
While libraries are "publishable" out of the box, adding tools like esbuild to your project requires creating custom executors, which involves defining a schema and a task runner in NodeJS.

**Maintenance of Project References**
TypeScript project references can be maintenance-heavy, especially in large workspaces, with the challenge lying in keeping the references array in each tsconfig.json file up to date. However, Nx includes a sync command that is automatically triggered before critical operations like building or serving a project.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about the Nx `enforce-module-boundaries` ESLint rule and tags constraints:

## Overview

You can declaratively define constraints using project tags and enforce them automatically through the @nx/enforce-module-boundaries ESLint rule for JavaScript/TypeScript projects.

## Tags and Constraints Structure

Nx enforces boundaries through a tag-based system where each library in your workspace is assigned one or more tags via its project.json file, and your ESLint configuration defines rules that govern which tags are allowed to depend on which other tags.

The depConstraints section represents an array of constraints, each consisting of sourceTag and onlyDependOnLibsWithTags properties.

## Constraint Requirements

A constraint must include sourceTag or allSourceTags, and the constraints are applied with AND logical operation - for a given source project the resulting constraints would be all that match its tags.

## How Tags Work

Tags typically carry two dimensions of information: scope (which domain or vertical the library belongs to) and type (what architectural layer or role the library plays).

## Dependency Rules

With proper constraints, scope:client projects can only depend on projects with scope:client or scope:shared, scope:admin projects can only depend on projects with scope:admin or scope:shared, meaning scope:client and scope:admin cannot depend on each other.

The rule configuration allows you to define multiple constraint dimensions and enforce complex architectural patterns in your monorepo.

## Nx Build Tools for TypeScript Libraries

### Available Options

If you choose tsc or swc, the result will be a buildable library using either tsc or swc as the compiler. If you choose rollup or vite, the result will be a buildable library using rollup or vite as the bundler.

Additionally, you can generate a buildable library using ESBuild as the bundler, which will use the @nx/esbuild:esbuild executor.

### Compiler Options

- **TSC**: By default, @nx/js uses TSC to compile libraries.
- **SWC**: You can convert to use SWC for faster compilation at any time with the convert-to-swc generator.

### Executor-Specific Configuration

For different build approaches, you can configure options in your `project.json`:

- **Rollup**: The @nx/rollup:rollup executor can be used as a bundler. You can also specify the compiler property in your project.json under the build target options to choose between SWC or Babel.

- **ESBuild**: You can specify whether you want to bundle your library or not in your project.json under the build target options, using the esbuildOptions property.

### Performance Improvements

The @nx/js:tsc batch implementation was introduced in Nx 16.6.0. The @nx/js:tsc executor supports running multiple tasks in a single process. When running in batch mode, the executor uses the TypeScript APIs for incremental builds. This results in a much faster build time when compared to the default implementation.

## Key Findings

**Current Nx Approach:**
Nx has released a brand new experience for Nx workspaces, moving away from historically relying on TypeScript's path aliases to connect packages. The new setup uses NPM/Yarn/PNPM/Bun workspaces combined with TypeScript project references, which is faster and more efficient in terms of memory use.

**Path Aliases in Monorepos:**
To configure path aliases, you can adjust the tsconfig.json file at the root of the monorepo in the compilerOptions.paths section, and individual tsconfig.json files can extend this base config to inherit these paths.

**Best Practices:**
It's critical to add aliases to the tsconfig.base.json file in the root of the monorepo, not in the tsconfig.json file found in individual apps. If you define TS path aliases in an individual project's tsconfig files, you should not define them also in the root tsconfig.base.json file because TypeScript does not merge the paths—the paths defined in the root file would be completely overwritten.

**When to Use Which Approach:**
For small projects or just for making imports pretty, path aliases are fine, but for most Nx monorepos, especially bigger ones, you should use TypeScript Project References. Going forward, the recommended approach is to use NPM, Yarn, PNPM, or Bun workspaces combined with TypeScript project references, which integrates more seamlessly with modern tooling.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive comparison of Nx, Turborepo, and Moon monorepo tools for 2025-2026:

## **Key Positioning**

Nx has significantly expanded its vision, evolving into what it calls a "Build Intelligence Platform" in 2025, making CI/CD more intelligent and proactive through AI integration. Turborepo is a high-performance task runner with a philosophy of minimalism and pure speed, focusing on understanding package.json script dependencies and executing tasks in parallel with aggressive caching. Moon is language agnostic, with initial support for Node.js and its ecosystem, and provides extensive configuration for customizing the tool to your needs.

## **Philosophy & Approach**

Nx offers a more comprehensive solution with advanced features and extensive tooling, while Turborepo provides a simpler, more focused approach with excellent build performance. Turborepo's configuration is simple with a single turbo.json file, and you can add it to an existing monorepo in under 10 minutes without forcing project restructuring.

## **Technical Advancements (2025-2026)**

A profound trend has been the strategic migration of core components to Rust, with Turborepo's journey to Rust beginning in late 2023 to extract maximum performance for hashing and graph traversal. Nx is following a similar path, with plans announced in late 2024 to migrate its core from TypeScript to Rust, targeting 2025 completion to improve speed, reduce package size, and eliminate Node.js runtime overheads.

## **Language Support**

Nx works with any programming language, framework and tooling, with its core written in Rust for speed and TypeScript for extensibility, allowing you to avoid adding package.json files for languages like Rust, Java, Go, and .NET. Turborepo only supports the Node.js ecosystem and provides very little configuration for customization.

## **When to Choose Each**

Choose Turborepo if your main problem is slow CI/CD and local builds, you have an existing monorepo without wanting costly migration, you have a senior disciplined team that can self-manage architecture, and you value minimalism and flexibility. Choose Nx if you're starting a new project and want solid structure from day zero, and your project is large, complex, and needs long-term maintainability.

Based on the web search results, here's comprehensive information about Nx affected, graph, run-many, caching, and CI setup for 2025:

## Core Concepts

To understand which projects are affected, Nx uses the Git history and the project graph. Git knows which files changed, and the Nx project graph knows which projects those files belong to.

## Affected Command

The affected command takes a base and head commit. The default base is your main branch, and the default head is your current file system. However, in CI, you need to customize these values.

The recommended approach is to set the base SHA to the latest successful commit on the main branch. This drastically improves the speed of your CI and reduces the amount of compute needed. This advantage is further enhanced when paired with remote caching and distribution.

## How Affected Works vs Caching

The affected graph answers "What needs to run?" while cache hits answer "Has this work already been done?". Combining both ensures that you skip unaffected projects entirely and skip execution for tasks with unchanged inputs.

## Run-Many and Parallelization

If you run nx run-many -t build or nx affected -t build, Nx will run all the specified tasks and their dependencies in parallel as much as possible.

## CI Setup and Caching Strategy

Using the nx affected command speeds up the first CI run for a PR and remote caching speeds up every CI run after that. It is rare for a task to be cached on the first run. However, if the PR doesn't pass in CI, or if you need to make a change for some reason, subsequent runs of that same PR will be able to reuse cached tasks.

## Distributed Task Execution (2025 Features)

Combining affected runs and remote caching with task distribution is key to maintaining low CI times. Nx Agents handles this distribution efficiently, avoiding the complexity and maintenance required if you were to set it up manually.

Tasks are picked up by agents based on the task's required processing time (from historical data) and task dependency/ordering (from the Nx graph). ## What is Enforce-Module-Boundaries?

The @nx/enforce-module-boundaries ESLint rule enables you to define strict rules for accessing resources between different projects in the repository, helping to prevent unplanned cross-dependencies.

## How It Works

Nx enforces boundaries through a tag-based system where each library in your workspace is assigned one or more tags via its project.json file, and your ESLint configuration defines rules that govern which tags are allowed to depend on which other tags.

## Effective Practices

The built-in solution from Nx is considered the least versatile and doesn't scale well as the number of projects in the monorepo grows, with this simplicity coming with limitations and making it the least flexible solution.

You can only apply rules at the library level by assigning tags in the project.json file, and if your project is structured differently and you need to apply rules at the sub-folder level, this is not possible.

# Enforce Module Boundaries Documentation Summary

## Overview
Nx provides mechanisms to maintain clean architecture by controlling dependencies between projects using tags and automated enforcement.

## Setting Up Tags

Projects are annotated with tags in their configuration files. The documentation shows three example tags: `scope:client`, `scope:admin`, and `scope:shared`.

**In package.json:**
```jsonc
{
  "nx": {
    "tags": ["scope:client"]
  }
}
```

**In project.json:**
```jsonc
{
  "tags": ["scope:client"]
}
```

## ESLint Configuration

After installing `@nx/eslint-plugin` and `@nx/devkit`, configure the `@nx/enforce-module-boundaries` rule.

Using flat config format, the rule accepts `depConstraints` as an array of constraint objects:

```javascript
{
  '@nx/enforce-module-boundaries': [
    'error',
    {
      allow: [],
      depConstraints: [
        {
          sourceTag: 'scope:shared',
          onlyDependOnLibsWithTags: ['scope:shared']
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Constraint Rules

The `sourceTag` identifies which projects are restricted, while `onlyDependOnLibsWithTags` specifies allowed dependencies.

**Tag Format Options:**

- **Wildcard (`*`)**: "allow all tags"
- **String**: Exact tag matching
- **Regex**: Pattern matching (e.g., `/^scope.*/`)
- **Glob**: Basic wildcard patterns (e.g., `scope:*`)

## Example Constraints

The documentation demonstrates preventing cross-scope dependencies:
- `scope:client` projects depend only on `scope:client` or `scope:shared`
- `scope:admin` projects depend only on `scope:admin` or `scope:shared`
- Result: "scope:client and scope:admin cannot depend on each other"

## Alternative Approach

For language-agnostic enforcement, the Conformance plugin checks dependencies during `nx conformance:check` (requires Nx Enterprise).

# Nx Inferred Tasks (Project Crystal) - Complete Documentation

## Overview

Nx plugins automatically detect tool configurations and infer tasks without manual setup. This "Project Crystal" feature, introduced in Nx 18, enables intelligent caching and task dependency management by analyzing existing configuration files.

## How Plugin Inference Works

Plugins follow a two-step process:

**Detection Phase**: The plugin searches for tool-specific configuration files (e.g., `webpack.config.js`, `vite.config.ts`) across the workspace.

**Task Creation**: Tasks are configured with names specified in `nx.json` plugin settings, using values extracted from the detected configuration files to determine caching behavior, inputs, outputs, and dependencies.

For example, the `@nx/webpack` plugin identifies webpack configurations and automatically infers cache settings based on build output destinations defined in those files.

## Inferred Task Properties

Plugins analyze tool configurations to automatically determine:

- **Command**: How the tool executes
- **Cacheability**: Whether outputs can be restored when inputs remain unchanged
- **Inputs**: Files and dependencies used to generate outputs
- **Outputs**: Results that get cached
- **Task Dependencies**: Other tasks that must complete first

## Configuration Precedence (Lowest to Highest Priority)

1. Inferred configurations from plugins
2. `targetDefaults` in `nx.json`
3. Project-specific configuration in `package.json` or `project.json`

Project-level settings override workspace defaults, which override plugin inference.

## Plugin Registration and Ordering

Plugins are processed in the order they appear in the `plugins` array within `nx.json`. When multiple plugins create identically-named tasks, the later plugin's version takes precedence. This allows deliberate override behavior when needed.

## Scoping Plugins to Specific Projects

Use `include` and `exclude` glob patterns to control which configuration files a plugin processes:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "plugin": "@nx/jest/plugin",
      "include": ["packages/**/*"],
      "exclude": ["**/*-e2e/**/*"]
    }
  ]
}
```

This approach enables applying different plugin options to various project subsets without registering plugins multiple times.

## Viewing Inferred Tasks

Display task configurations using the command-line interface:

```shell
nx show project my-project --web
```

This reveals all inferred task properties, their source configuration files, and which plugins created them.

## Customizing Inferred Tasks

Three methods exist for customization:

**Workspace-Level**: Modify `targetDefaults` in `nx.json` to adjust settings across multiple projects.

**Project-Level**: Update individual project files to override specific tasks.

**Plugin Scoping**: Use `include`/`exclude` patterns to limit which projects a plugin affects.

Detailed customization guides cover configuring inputs, outputs, task pipelines, and command arguments.

## Legacy Workspace Migration

Existing workspaces receive `useInferencePlugins: false` during upgrades, preserving traditional executor-based task definitions. New projects still use explicit executors until inference is enabled. Repositories can gradually adopt inferred tasks through migration recipes provided in Nx documentation.

Even fully-migrated projects benefit from `project.json` files for overriding inferred options and defining non-inferable tasks (like TypeScript batch mode operations).

# Create-NX-Workspace Command Reference

## Usage
```bash
npx create-nx-workspace [name] [options]
```

## Core Workspace Types

The `--workspaceType` option defines your project structure:

- **integrated**: Monorepo structure with centralized configuration
- **package-based**: Uses package manager workspaces with distributed configs
- **standalone**: Single application setup

## TypeScript Preset Overview

The `ts` preset provides "a basic integrated style repository starting with TypeScript configured but no projects." This serves as a minimal foundation for teams wanting to build custom project structures. The `ts-standalone` variant offers a single TypeScript application instead.

## All Available Presets

The framework includes 21 presets spanning multiple technology ecosystems:

**Frontend frameworks**: angular, angular-monorepo, angular-standalone, react, react-monorepo, react-standalone, vue, vue-monorepo, vue-standalone, next, nextjs-standalone, nuxt, nuxt-standalone, web-components

**Backend/Full-stack**: express, nest, node-monorepo, node-standalone

**Mobile**: react-native, expo

**Foundational**: apps, npm, ts, ts-standalone

## Key Configuration Options

| Category | Notable Flags |
|----------|--------------|
| **Package Management** | `--packageManager` (bun, npm, pnpm, yarn; default: npm) |
| **Testing** | `--unitTestRunner` (jest, vitest, none), `--e2eTestRunner` (playwright, cypress, none) |
| **Version Control** | `--skipGit`, `--useGitHub`, `--skipGitHubPush` |
| **Framework-Specific** | `--nextAppDir`, `--nextSrcDir`, `--routing`, `--ssr`, `--style` |
| **Angular-Specific** | `--standaloneApi`, `--zoneless`, `--prefix` |
| **Project Structure** | `--workspaces` (default: true), `--useProjectJson` |

## Additional Options

- `--aiAgents`: Configure AI tool integration (claude, copilot, cursor, gemini, etc.)
- `--docker`: Generate Dockerfile for Node API
- `--nxCloud`/`--ci`: Enable CI/CD provider integration
- `--interactive`: Enable preset selection mode (default: true)
- `--verbose`: Detailed logging output

# Monorepo Tooling Comparison: Turborepo, Nx, and Lerna in 2026

## Key Differentiators

**Turborepo (Vercel)**
- *Strengths*: Fast task execution with `--affected` flag for selective CI runs; seamless remote caching via Vercel integration (free for linked repos); composable configuration system
- *Weaknesses*: Potential vendor lock-in with Vercel ecosystem; plugin ecosystem remains JavaScript-centric
- *Best for*: Teams using Vercel infrastructure; projects prioritizing speed and simplicity

**Nx (Nrwl)**
- *Strengths*: "Build Intelligence Platform" with AI integration via MCP server; self-healing CI with task analytics and flaky test detection; Nx Daemon eliminates cold-start problems; graph visualization
- *Weaknesses*: Steeper learning curve; higher initial configuration complexity
- *Best for*: Large, polyglot monorepos requiring deep observability and intelligent automation

**Lerna**
- *Strengths*: OIDC trusted publishing (eliminates static npm tokens); leverages underlying Nx execution engine; modernized tooling
- *Weaknesses*: Removed legacy commands like `lerna add`; requires native workspace configuration
- *Best for*: Multi-package publishing workflows with security-focused CI/CD pipelines

## TypeScript Library Projects

The article doesn't specifically address library-focused recommendations, but suggests:
- Leverage composable configurations for shared build processes
- Implement dependency graph analysis to identify circular dependencies
- Use remote caching for consistent artifact handling across environments

## Reality Check

The author notes: "For very small projects, the 'monorepo tax' in terms of learning curve and configuration can still outweigh the benefits," and warns about "Debugging Remote Cache Issues" when inputs are misconfigured.

# TypeScript Project Linking in Nx: Complete Documentation

## Overview

Nx supports two approaches for linking TypeScript projects within monorepos: **package manager workspaces** and **TypeScript path aliases**. The workspace method has become the recommended approach because it leverages native Node module resolution rather than relying solely on TypeScript compilation.

## The Problem with Relative Paths

Instead of writing:
```ts
import { someFunction } from '../../teamA/otherProject';
```

The better practice is to reference local projects as npm packages:
```ts
import { someFunction } from '@myorg/otherProject';
```

This decouples imports from folder structure, making refactoring easier and improving developer experience.

## Package Manager Workspaces Configuration

### Root Setup
Each package manager requires slightly different configuration:

- **npm/yarn/bun**: Define `"workspaces": ["apps/*", "packages/*"]` in root `package.json`
- **pnpm**: Use `pnpm-workspace.yaml` with packages property instead

### Dependency Declaration
Local projects should be listed in `devDependencies` with version specifiers:
- npm: `"*"`
- yarn/bun/pnpm: `"workspace:*"`

This prevents libraries from being bundled twice in production builds.

## TypeScript Project References

When using workspaces, enable TypeScript project references for performance gains:

**Root tsconfig.base.json** requirements:
- Set `"composite": true` and `"declaration": true`
- Omit `paths` property
- Include `references` array with all projects

**Individual project tsconfig.json** structure:
- Extend `tsconfig.base.json`
- List project dependencies in `references`
- Maintain separate `tsconfig.lib.json` and `tsconfig.spec.json` files

## Performance Metrics

TypeScript project references provide substantial improvements. According to benchmarking data: "Typecheck without using project references: 186 seconds, max memory 6.14 GB" versus "Typecheck with all `.tsbuildinfo` files created: 25 seconds, max memory 429 MB."

The `.tsbuildinfo` cache files enable incremental compilation, allowing subsequent runs to process only modified projects while reusing cached type information for unchanged ones.

## TypeScript Path Aliases Approach

As an alternative to workspaces, define all paths in `tsconfig.base.json`:

```jsonc
"paths": {
  "@myorg/shared-ui": ["packages/shared-ui/src/index.ts"]
}
```

**Important limitation**: Project-specific path aliases override root configuration entirely—you cannot combine both approaches within the same tsconfig inheritance chain.

## Key Differences

| Aspect | Workspaces | Path Aliases |
|--------|-----------|--------------|
| Module Resolution | Native Node | TypeScript-based |
| Configuration | package.json/yaml | tsconfig.json |
| Performance Caching | `.tsbuildinfo` files | Limited |
| Ecosystem Alignment | Modern standard | Legacy approach |

# Three Approaches to Enforcing Module Boundaries in Nx Monorepos

## 1. Nx Module Boundaries (Built-in Solution)

**Configuration Example:**
```json
"@nx/enforce-module-boundaries": [
  "error",
  {
    "depConstraints": [
      {
        "sourceTag": "type:feature",
        "onlyDependOnLibsWithTags": [
          "type:feature",
          "type:model",
          "type:data-access",
          "type:ui",
          "type:util"
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

**Tag Pattern:**
Libraries use multidimensional tags like `scope:learnings` and `type:data-access` assigned in `project.json`.

**Pros:**
- "It's a built-in solution, it doesn't require additional external dependencies"
- Integrated with ESLint for seamless linting workflows

**Cons:**
- Limited to project-level rules; cannot enforce constraints at subfolder levels
- Lacks support for complex architectural patterns

**Best For:** Small to medium monorepos with straightforward dependency structures

---

## 2. Dependency Cruiser

**Configuration Example:**
```javascript
{
  name: "no-cross-domains",
  severity: "error",
  from: { path: "^libs/(?!(shared))([^/]+)" },
  to: { path: "^libs/(?!(shared))", pathNot: "^libs/$1" }
}
```

**Advanced Rule Pattern:**
Can enforce "truly shared" libraries: "Each shared lib's index.ts must be imported by at least two other first-level libs"

**Pros:**
- Framework-agnostic and highly flexible
- Detects circular dependencies, dead code, and orphaned modules
- Generates visual dependency graphs showing violations
- Supports folder-level rules independent of project tags

**Cons:**
- Operates separately from ESLint
- Steeper learning curve due to extended capabilities

**Best For:** Large monorepos requiring code-quality analysis beyond dependency enforcement

---

## 3. Sheriff

**Configuration Example:**
```typescript
modules: {
  'libs/<scope>/feature-<feature>/src': ['scope:<scope>', 'type:feature'],
  'libs/<scope>/<type>/src': ['scope:<scope>', 'type:<type>'],
},
depRules: {
  'scope:*': [sameTag, 'scope:shared'],
  'type:feature': ['type:feature', 'type:model', /* ... */]
}
```

**Pattern Innovation:**
Uses placeholders and automatic tagging to minimize configuration boilerplate.

**Pros:**
- Framework-agnostic with folder-level granularity
- Reduced configuration repetition through placeholders
- Optional ESLint integration
- Fine-grained rule definitions without relying on external tags

**Cons:**
- Requires understanding of automatic tagging concepts
- Lacks broader code-quality analysis features

**Best For:** Growing monorepos needing flexible rules without verbose configuration

---

## Comparative Recommendations

| Scenario | Recommendation | Rationale |
|----------|---|---|
| Starting monorepo | Nx Module Boundaries | Minimal setup overhead |
| Need code quality insights | Dependency Cruiser | Identifies shared-but-unused modules, circular deps |
| Scale with minimal config | Sheriff | Automatic tagging reduces maintenance burden |
| Multi-domain architecture | Dependency Cruiser or Sheriff | Both support cross-domain validation rules |

The author concludes: "I'd lean toward Dependency Cruiser if I needed to check additional things, such as whether a module is 'shared enough'" or prefer Sheriff for scaling without configuration bloat.

# Complete Guide: Monorepo Setup with PNPM Workspaces and Nx

## Initial Setup

**Create your workspace structure:**
```bash
mkdir pnpm-mono
cd pnpm-mono
pnpm init
git init
```

Add a `.gitignore` file excluding `node_modules`, `dist`, and `build` directories.

## Monorepo Configuration

**Create folders for your projects:**
```bash
mkdir apps packages
```

**Configure PNPM with `pnpm-workspace.yaml`:**
```yaml
packages:
  - 'apps/*'
  - 'packages/*'
```

This designates an app-centric structure where `apps/` contains deployable applications and `packages/` contains shared libraries.

## Application Setup

Add a Remix application (or any framework):
```bash
cd apps
npx create-remix@latest
```

Ensure the `apps/my-remix-app/package.json` includes a `name` field, as PNPM requires it for filtering commands.

## Shared Library Package

Create a `packages/shared-ui/` directory with its own `package.json`:

```json
{
  "private": true,
  "name": "shared-ui",
  "main": "dist/index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "rm -rf dist && tsc"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "react": "^17.0.2"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "typescript": "^4.6.4"
  }
}
```

Include a `tsconfig.json` with appropriate compiler settings for your components.

## Dependency Linking

Link the shared library to your app:
```bash
pnpm add shared-ui --filter my-remix-app --workspace
```

This adds `"shared-ui": "workspace:*"` to your app's dependencies, creating local symlinks.

## Nx Integration

**Install Nx at the workspace root:**
```bash
pnpm add nx -D -w
```

**Create `nx.json` configuration:**
```json
{
  "tasksRunnerOptions": {
    "default": {
      "runner": "nx/tasks-runners/default",
      "options": {
        "cacheableOperations": ["build", "test"]
      }
    }
  },
  "namedInputs": {
    "noMarkdown": ["!{projectRoot}/**/*.md"]
  },
  "targetDefaults": {
    "build": {
      "inputs": ["noMarkdown", "^noMarkdown"],
      "dependsOn": ["^build"]
    },
    "dev": {
      "dependsOn": ["^build"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Key Configuration Elements

**Caching:** The `cacheableOperations` array specifies which tasks should be cached. Nx computes input hashes and restores matching outputs, dramatically reducing build times on subsequent runs.

**Named Inputs:** Reusable glob patterns prevent cache invalidation from irrelevant file changes (like markdown documentation).

**Task Dependencies:** The `dependsOn` property with `^` notation ensures dependent projects' builds run before consuming projects, eliminating manual build ordering.

## Running Tasks

Execute single project tasks:
```bash
npx nx build shared-ui
npx nx dev my-remix-app
```

Run across all projects:
```bash
npx nx run-many --target=build --all
```

## Benefits Provided

- **Speed:** Computation caching eliminates redundant work; cached builds complete in milliseconds
- **Task Orchestration:** Automatic dependency resolution respects build pipeline requirements
- **Selective Execution:** The `affected` command runs only tasks for changed projects
- **Visualization:** `npx nx graph` displays project dependencies interactively

This approach combines PNPM's lightweight package management with Nx's sophisticated task scheduling, creating an efficient development environment for monorepo projects.

# TypeScript/JS Executors in Nx

Based on the documentation provided, here are the available executors:

## `tsc` - TypeScript Compiler

**Key Options:**
- `main` (required): Entry point file
- `outputPath` (required): Output directory for compiled files
- `tsConfig` (required): Path to TypeScript configuration
- `clean`: Remove previous output before building (default: true)
- `generatePackageJson`: Generate package.json in output (default: true)
- `transformers`: Apply TypeScript transformer plugins
- `watch`: Rebuild on file changes (default: false)

**When to Use:**
Use for standard TypeScript compilation with native TS tooling. Ideal when you need transformer plugins or incremental builds via batch mode (available since Nx 16.6.0).

**Configuration Example:**
```json
{
  "build": {
    "executor": "@nx/js:tsc",
    "options": {
      "outputPath": "dist/libs/ts-lib",
      "main": "libs/ts-lib/src/index.ts",
      "tsConfig": "libs/ts-lib/tsconfig.lib.json",
      "transformers": ["@nestjs/swagger/plugin"]
    }
  }
}
```

## `swc` - SWC Compiler

**Key Options:**
- `main` (required): Entry point file
- `outputPath` (required): Output directory
- `tsConfig` (required): TypeScript configuration path
- `swcrc`: Custom SWC configuration file path
- `assets`: Static assets to copy
- `clean`: Remove previous output (default: true)
- `watch`: Rebuild on changes (default: false)

**When to Use:**
Choose SWC for faster compilation speeds compared to TypeScript. Supports custom `.swcrc` configurations for different build environments.

**Configuration Example:**
```json
{
  "build": {
    "executor": "@nx/js:swc",
    "options": {
      "outputPath": "dist/libs/ts-lib",
      "main": "libs/ts-lib/src/index.ts",
      "tsConfig": "libs/ts-lib/tsconfig.lib.json",
      "swcrc": "libs/ts-lib/.dev.swcrc"
    },
    "configurations": {
      "production": {
        "swcrc": "libs/ts-lib/.prod.swcrc"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

---

**Note:** The provided documentation does not include esbuild or rollup executor details, only tsc and swc are fully documented.

Vitest provides a way to define multiple project configurations within a single Vitest process. This feature is particularly useful for monorepo setups but can also be used to run tests with different configurations, such as resolve.alias, plugins, ...

The official Nx documentation provides generators like `nx g @nx/vitest:configuration` to set up Vitest in your projects with appropriate framework-specific options.

# Nx Caching: Complete Documentation Summary

## Core Caching Mechanism

Nx uses **computation hashing** to determine cache validity. As stated in the documentation, "As long as the computation hash is the same, the output of running the task is the same."

The computation hash incorporates:
- Source files of the project and dependencies
- Global configuration settings
- External dependency versions
- Runtime values (e.g., Node version)
- CLI command flags

## Cache Lookup and Storage

The caching workflow follows this sequence:

1. Nx computes the hash for a task
2. Checks the local cache first
3. If missing, queries the remote cache (if configured)
4. On cache hit: retrieves and replays outputs with restored files
5. On cache miss: executes the task, then stores results locally and remotely

## What Gets Cached

Three primary elements are cached:

- **Terminal output**: Logs, warnings, and errors from task execution
- **Task artifacts**: Files defined in the `outputs` property (build results, test reports, etc.)
- **Computation hash**: The hash value itself (not the actual inputs)

## Defining Inputs and Outputs

**Outputs** are specified in project configuration files:

```json
"targets": {
  "build": {
    "outputs": ["{projectRoot}/dist"]
  }
}
```

**Inputs** define what factors affect the cache hash. By default, this includes all project files (`{projectRoot}/**/*`), but can be customized to exclude items like markdown files.

## Cache Invalidation

The cache invalidates when any input factor changes—source code modifications, dependency version updates, CLI flags, or environment variables. This granular approach ensures cache accuracy across different scenarios.

# Configuring Vite in Nx Workspaces: Complete Guide

## Core Setup Requirements

The Nx Vite plugin automates configuration, but manual setup requires several key components:

**TypeScript Path Resolution:** Implement the `nxViteTsPaths()` plugin to ensure "your TypeScript paths are resolved correctly in your monorepo."

**Root Directory Configuration:** Set `root: __dirname,` in your config object for proper path resolution across monorepo structures.

## Output Directory Management

Configure `outDir` relative to the workspace root. For a project at `apps/my-app`, use `../../dist/apps/my-app`; for `my-app` at the root level, use `../dist/my-app`.

## Library-Specific Configuration

Libraries require the `vite-plugin-dts` plugin to generate TypeScript declaration files. Two diagnostic approaches exist:

- **Skip Diagnostics:** Set `skipDiagnostics: true` to accelerate builds, though files with type errors won't emit `.d.ts` files
- **Enable Diagnostics:** Set `skipDiagnostics: false` to "make sure that all the files are type checked"

## Asset Management

Use `nxCopyAssetsPlugin` from `@nx/vite` for assets outside `publicDir` that need inclusion in output folders.

## Vitest Configuration

Essential test settings include:
```
- globals: true
- environment: 'jsdom'
- reporters: ['default']
- cache directory paths relative to root
- coverage directory configuration
```

## Framework-Specific Plugins

React projects require `@vitejs/plugin-react`; Vue projects require `@vitejs/plugin-vue`.

## File Replacement Strategy

The `replaceFiles()` plugin from `@nx/vite/plugins/rollup-replace-files.plugin` enables environment-specific file substitution during builds, useful for production configurations.

# Nx Affected Command: Complete Documentation

## Overview

The `nx affected` command identifies and runs tasks only on projects impacted by changes, significantly improving CI performance. As stated in the documentation: "Using this command, Nx determines the minimum set of **projects that are affected by the change**" and executes tasks exclusively on those projects.

## Core Functionality

When executing `nx affected -t <task>`, Nx performs three key steps:

1. Analyzes Git history to identify modified files in your pull request
2. Consults the project graph to determine which projects own those files
3. Calculates downstream dependencies to identify all affected projects

The documentation notes: "This drastically improves the speed of your CI and reduces the amount of compute needed."

## Basic Usage

```shell
nx affected -t <task>
nx affected -t test
nx affected -t build
nx graph --affected  # visualize affected projects
```

## CI Configuration

For continuous integration environments, customize the Git commit range:

```shell
nx affected -t build --base=origin/main --head=$PR_BRANCH_NAME
nx affected -t build --base=origin/main~1 --head=origin/main
```

Environment variable approach:

```shell
NX_BASE=origin/main~1
NX_HEAD=origin/main
```

**Best practice**: Set the base SHA to "the latest successful commit on the `main` branch," ensuring all changes since the last successful CI run are evaluated.

## File Exclusion

Two mechanisms prevent files from triggering affected calculations:

- Patterns in `.gitignore` are automatically ignored
- Patterns in an optional `.nxignore` file are ignored

## Advanced Configuration

### Dependency Update Handling

Configure how lock file changes affect project status:

```json
{
  "pluginsConfig": {
    "@nx/js": {
      "projectsAffectedByDependencyUpdates": "auto"
    }
  }
}
```

Options: `auto`, `all`, or custom project specifiers (default: `all`)

### Non-Git Environments

Use the `--files` flag to specify changed files manually:

```shell
nx affected --files=path/to/file
```

## Enhancement Opportunities

# Nx 2025 Year-in-Review: Key Highlights

## Major Features Shipped

**Build Intelligence Platform**: Nx evolved into a unified system combining build systems, CI orchestration, and AI integration to eliminate development bottlenecks.

**Self-Healing CI**: When pull requests fail, Nx analyzes root causes and posts fix suggestions directly in PRs. The platform achieves approximately 60% acceptance rates on suggested fixes, even in large monorepos.

**Workspace-Aware AI Integration**: Two tools enhance LLM capabilities:
- The Nx MCP server provides deep access to workspace structure, dependencies, and task configurations
- Terminal integration enables real-time error analysis and immediate fix suggestions

**Enterprise Analytics**: 
- Task Analytics tracks performance trends over time to identify regressions
- Flaky Task Analytics prioritizes fixing tests that waste the most time
- Agent Resource Usage provides process-level CI visibility

## Pattern Recommendations & Configuration Changes

**TypeScript Project References** became the default configuration for new workspaces after proving to significantly accelerate development cycles.

**Polyglot Workspace Support**: Native support expanded to include Gradle, Maven, and .NET alongside JavaScript tooling, enabling developers to manage diverse tech stacks within single repositories.

## Developer Experience Enhancements

- Terminal UI for viewing multiple simultaneous tasks
- Continuous tasks enabling non-blocking pipelines
- IDE integration in VSCode and JetBrains with direct CI failure notifications
- Visual migration guidance within Nx Console

## 2026 Roadmap Priorities

Incoming features include:
- LLM code mode for improved context management
- Claude Code plugin integration with Nx plugins
- Specialized AI agents for migrations and code generation
- Subgraph creation to reduce unnecessary dependencies
- Strict cache validation guarantees

# Nx 22 Release: Key Features and Changes

## Major New Features

**Self-Healing CI**: Analyzes failing PRs and suggests automatic fixes. Developers can review, apply locally, or accept changes pushed directly to PRs. Currently supports GitHub with GitLab testing.

**Nx Console Enhancements**: Integrates status updates for PRs and CI fixes directly into IDEs (VS Code, JetBrains). Includes Migrate UI for visual migration approvals and automatic AI configuration validation.

**Polygraph**: Enterprise solution enabling visibility across multiple repositories, whether or not they use Nx, helping organizations "identify duplicate dependencies, enforce architectural patterns, and understand cross-repository impacts."

**Graph Visualization Rewrite**: Handles repositories of any size through composite mode rendering, preventing crashes in workspaces with thousands of projects while improving navigation.

**Terminal UI Improvements**: Replaced pagination with smooth scrolling, enhanced title styling, better task filtering, and prevents unwanted scrolling during interactions.

## Polyglot Support Expansion

**Maven Plugin** (@nx/maven): Experimental support bringing Java ecosystem integration with automatic project detection, intelligent caching, and distributed task execution.

**Dotnet Plugin** (@nx/dotnet): Enterprise-ready .NET support with automatic discovery of projects and inference of build, test, and watch targets. Integrates existing project files while enabling remote caching and distributed execution.

**Gradle Performance**: Achieved "59.6% reduction in time" on Spring Boot CI pipeline (from 104 to 42 minutes) through batch task processing.

## Dependency Management

**pnpm Catalog Support**: Automatic recognition and formatting of catalog definitions during migrations. Centralized version management across monorepo projects using the `catalog:` protocol.

## AI Integration

Expanded AI agent support through dual API design (developers and AI), improved configuration validation via `configure-ai-agents` command, and planned Claude Skills feature support.

## Breaking Changes

- Database-backed caching now standard (NX_DISABLE_DB removed)
- CreateNodes V1 removed; migration to createNodesV2 required
- Deprecated webpack/rspack options removed
- Legacy TypeScript plugin behavior changed
- Nx Release legacy versioning removed
- Inlining feature removed from tsc/swc executors
- npm legacy peer deps no longer forced
- Migrations prior to Nx 20 removed
